To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
7α-hydrxylase activity is much higher in the rat compared to the hamster, and that the rat is able to induce 7α-hydroyxylase in response to dietary cholesterol, whereas the hamster cannot.

the rat and the hamster have similar responses to dietary cholesterol in the liver, i.e. they both suppress hepatic cholesterol synthesis when fed high cholesterol diets, but the rat is much more resistant to the choleste- rolemic effects of dietary cholesterol because of its ability to induce hepatic 7a-hydroxylases and increase bile acid synthesis.

The rat is able to adapt its bile acid and cholesterol synthetic capacity to a wide range of sterol intakes with little change in LDL levels, whereas the hamster responds to dietary sterol with a large change in LDL levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of hepatic cholesterol and bile acid metabolism in the hamster and rat.
the mechanisms by which animals adapt to variations in dietary sterol.
the molecular mechanisms by which cholesterol homeostasis is maintained and how it is perturbed by diet.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the hamster has an impaired ability to adapt to fluctuations in dietary sterol, which results in a marked increase in plasma LDL cholesterol levels in response to a modest increase in dietary cholesterol intake.
the rat and the hamster differ in their sensitivity to dietary cholesterol because of differences in the basal level of expression and regulation of hepatic 7 α -hydroxylase activity.

the rat is more resistant to the hypercholesterolemic effect of dietary cholesterol than the hamster because the rat is able to maintain hepatic 7-hydroxylation of cholesterol and bile acid synthesis at a higher rate than the hamster, which is able, in contrast, to maintain bile acid and cholesterol syntheses at low rates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hamster is much more sensitive to the effects of dietary cholesterol on plasma LDL concentrations because of the low basal level and lack of induction of hepatic 7-hydroxylating enzymes.
the hamster, which has a low basal 7α-ho- xylase activity, does not adapt well to a change in sterol balance and therefore is more sensitive than the highly adaptable rat to dietary cholesterol.
the hamster has a lower basal rate of bile acid and sterol synthesis, and a lower rate of bile acid synthesis in response to dietary cholesterol, than does the rat.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rat is a poor model to study the effects of dietary cholesterol on LDL metabolism because of its unique capacity to adapt to large changes in sterol intake.
the hamster is an excellent model for the human in terms of the response to dietary cholesterol.
there are species differences in the regulation of hepatic 7-hydroxylases.
